spans.assertion: the analysis examined whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned vs light-skinned players using 146,028 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues
logistic regression with marginal standardization was used, controlling for position, league, player characteristics, games played, and yellow cards

dark-skinned players were found to have a 0.18 percentage point higher probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players (95% CI [0.01,0.36]pp, p=0.034), with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.15 (95% CI [1.01,1.31])
the hypothesis is concluded to be supported by the data, with the effect described as small in absolute terms but statistically significant and a meaningful 15% relative increase
the point estimate for the adjusted risk difference was 0.18 percentage points (0.0018 probability scale)
the 95% confidence interval for the risk difference was [0.0125, 0.3566] percentage points
the two-sided p-value was 0.0344 against alpha of 0.05

after adjusting for position, league, age, height, weight, games, and yellow cards, dark-skinned players have a 0.18pp higher absolute probability of a red card, about 15% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline rate of 1.22%
the 95% CI excludes zero and the p-value 0.034 is below 0.05, taken as evidence against the null hypothesis of no difference
the point estimate for the adjusted odds ratio was 1.1541
the 95% CI for the odds ratio was [1.0103, 1.3125]
dark-skinned players have 15.4% higher odds of a red card after covariate adjustment, and the CI just excludes 1.0 indicating significance at 0.05
the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad, with N = 115,603 dyads
each observation represents all encounters between a specific player and a specific referee
the dataset contains 1,419 unique players
the dataset contains 2,904 unique referees
the total dyads in the dataset was 146,028
dyads with skin tone data numbered 124,621, or 85.3% of total
the final analysis sample was 115,603 dyads, a 79.2% retention rate
21,407 dyads were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no player photo) and 9,018 dyads were excluded for missing covariates (position, height, or weight)
anyRedCard was defined as a binary indicator for whether the player received at least one red card from that referee across all games in the dyad
there were 1,455 dyads with red cards, 1.26% of the sample
darkSkin was defined as a binary indicator based on the average skin tone rating from two independent raters
dark skin was coded as 1 if average skin tone rating was >= 0.5, including 'neither dark nor light', 'dark', and 'very dark' categories
light skin was coded as 0 if average skin tone rating was < 0.5, including 'very light' and 'light' categories
the original skin tone scale ran from 0 (very light) to 1.0 (very dark) in 0.25 increments
the distribution was 89,107 light skin dyads (77.1%) and 26,496 dark skin dyads (22.9%)
position was included as a categorical covariate with 12 levels, with Attacking Midfielder as reference
position was included because different positions may have different red card risks due to playing style and referee proximity
league country was included as a categorical covariate with 4 levels, with England as reference
league country was included because different leagues may have different refereeing standards
age was included as a continuous covariate (mean 27.1, SD 4.4)
age was included because older players may play differently or be perceived differently
height was included as a continuous covariate (mean 182.1cm, SD 6.8)
height was included because physical characteristics may influence play style
weight was included as a continuous covariate (mean 76.4kg, SD 7.2)
weight was included because physical characteristics may influence play style
games (number of games in the dyad) was included as a continuous covariate (mean 2.9, SD 3.4)
games was included because more exposure increases opportunity for red cards and it controls for differential encounter rates
yellow cards (number in the dyad) was included as a continuous covariate (mean 0.40, SD 0.82)
yellow cards was included as a proxy for player behavior/aggressiveness, since players with more yellow cards likely play more aggressively
the model type used was logistic regression
the model formula regressed logit(P(anyRedCard)) on darkSkin plus position, leagueCountry, age, height, weight, games, and yellowCards
maximum likelihood was used as the estimation method
model fit was McFadden pseudo R² = 0.073, log-likelihood = -7241.4, AIC = 14524.8
marginal standardization (g-computation/standardization) was the method used to calculate the risk difference
the logistic regression model was fit on the observed data
a counterfactual dataset was created setting all observations to darkSkin = 1
a counterfactual dataset was created setting all observations to darkSkin = 0
probabilities were predicted under each counterfactual scenario
the average difference E[P(Y=1|darkSkin=1,X)] - E[P(Y=1|darkSkin=0,X)] was calculated
marginal standardization is claimed to provide a population-average causal effect estimate on the probability scale
a parametric bootstrap with 5,000 iterations was used to compute standard errors and confidence intervals
coefficient vectors were drawn from a multivariate normal distribution N(β̂, Σ̂)
for each draw, the risk difference and odds ratio were calculated
the percentile method (2.5th/97.5th percentiles) was used for the 95% CI
the bootstrap approach is justified as accounting for uncertainty in all model parameters and being appropriate for complex non-linear functions of parameters
the bootstrap method assumes asymptotic normality of coefficient estimates and does not account for clustering by player or referee
standard logistic regression was used without an explicit clustering structure
standard errors do not account for within-player or within-referee correlation
standard errors may be somewhat underestimated and p-values may be anti-conservative as a result
given the large number of clusters and balanced cluster sizes, bias is judged likely modest, and the parametric bootstrap is said to provide some robustness
a more conservative analysis using cluster-robust standard errors or GEE would have been preferable but was computationally prohibitive, so it was not done
no transformations were applied to the continuous variables (age, height, weight, games, yellowCards); they were used on the original scale
skin tone was dichotomized at the median threshold of 0.5
complete case analysis (listwise deletion) was used for missing data
the analysis assumes data are missing completely at random or missing at random conditional on included covariates
skin tone was missing for 14.7% of cases (players without photos)
position was missing for 6.8% among those with skin tone
height was missing for 0.04% among those with skin tone
weight was missing for 0.6% among those with skin tone

spans.assertion: the unadjusted P(red card | light skin) was 1.23%
the unadjusted P(red card | dark skin) was 1.35%
the unadjusted difference was 0.12 percentage points
the adjusted effect (0.18pp) is larger than the unadjusted effect, suggesting confounders (particularly position and games played) partially mask the skin tone effect

spans.assertion: an alternative dichotomization was tested: very dark skin (>= 0.75) vs. others (< 0.75)
under the alternative dichotomization, coefficient = 0.158, OR = 1.17, p = 0.044
the effect is concluded to persist and strengthen slightly under the more stringent dark-skin definition, supporting robustness of findings
games was found to be a strong positive predictor of red cards (β=0.120, p<0.001)
yellow cards was found to be a strong positive predictor of red cards (β=0.085, p<0.001), interpreted as reflecting aggressive play
Center Backs were found to have the highest red card risk (OR=2.60 vs. Attacking Midfielders)
France and Spain were found to have higher red card rates than England; Germany was similar to England
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players is concluded to be supported by the data

the 95% CI [0.01,0.36]pp excluding zero is cited as evidence of precision
the two-sided p-value (0.034) being below 0.05 is cited as evidence of statistical significance

the strength of evidence is characterized as moderate because although statistically significant, the effect is small in absolute terms and the CI is relatively wide
